I couldn't get Alberta's child poverty rate, so I don't have a figure to give you.

Statistics Canada's website has been blocking automated requests since November 2026. The table lookup I needed timed out three times, and the search call was refused outright. I didn't want to give you a number from memory.

Alberta's rate should be in Statistics Canada table 11-10-0135-01, "Low income statistics by age, gender and economic family type". It was last updated 2026-04-29 and runs through 2024. In that table, pick Alberta, the age group "under 18 years", and the Market Basket Measure. That measure is Canada's official poverty line, and the 2023 base has been the official one since November 2025. A browser isn't blocked, so you can open the table directly. The other measures in the table (LIM-AT and LICO) give different rates, so check which one you're reading.

```json
{"values": [], "sources": [{"publisher": "Statistics Canada", "id": "11-10-0135-01"}], "not_published": false, "abstain": true, "abstain_reason": "Statistics Canada's site blocks automated requests (Cloudflare bot check) and the table metadata lookup timed out repeatedly, so the Alberta under-18 rate could not be retrieved or checked."}
```

I couldn't retrieve Alberta's average wage for provincial public administration, so I have no figure to give you. Statistics Canada's table service (the metadata endpoint, HTTP 500) failed on repeated tries. I can't identify the right series without that metadata, and I won't estimate from memory.

The right source is the Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours (SEPH). It reports average weekly earnings for Provincial and territorial public administration (NAICS 912), by province.
- **Monthly:** table 14-10-0203-01, latest reference period August 2026, released 2026-10-29.
- **Annual:** table 14-10-0204-01, latest reference year 2025 (the table's end date is January 2025).

Table 14-10-0064 is the wrong source. It only goes down to the broad "Public administration" sector, not provincial administration.

Once the service is back, I can look up the Alberta / NAICS 912 vector and pull the latest value. Retrying in a few minutes should work.

```json
{"values": [{"name": "Latest monthly SEPH reference period (table 14-10-0203-01)", "value": "2026-08", "unit": "month", "period": "2026-08"}, {"name": "SEPH monthly release date", "value": "2026-10-29", "unit": "date", "period": "2026-10-29"}], "sources": [{"publisher": "Statistics Canada", "id": "14-10-0203-01"}, {"publisher": "Statistics Canada", "id": "14-10-0204-01"}], "not_published": false, "abstain": true, "abstain_reason": "Statistics Canada's getCubeMetadata endpoint returned HTTP 500 (and one call timed out), so I couldn't identify the Alberta / NAICS 912 vector or retrieve the earnings value."}
```

In 2024, the average total income of people in Alberta aged 15 and over was **$66,100**. This figure is before tax and excludes people with zero income. It is a per-person figure, not household or family income. The median was $48,100. The average is higher because high earners pull it up.

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 11-10-0239-01 (Canadian Income Survey), released 2026-04-29. The vectors are v107680657 for the average and v107680658 for the median.

This is general information, not financial advice.

```json
{"values":[{"name":"Average total income, Alberta, persons 15+, all genders (excluding zeros)","value":66100,"unit":"dollars (current)","period":"2024"},{"name":"Median total income, Alberta, persons 15+ (excluding zeros)","value":48100,"unit":"dollars (current)","period":"2024"}],"sources":[{"publisher":"Statistics Canada","id":"11-10-0239-01 (v107680657, v107680658)"}],"not_published":false,"abstain":false,"abstain_reason":""}
```

I couldn't find an Alberta poverty rate for people with disabilities. Statistics Canada's table on this topic, 11-10-0090-01 (Poverty and low-income statistics by disability status), covers Canada only. Its geography dimension has no provinces. The Canadian Survey on Disability tables I searched had no provincial poverty figure either. I didn't estimate one.

The closest published figure is national. In 2024, 12.6% of persons with disabilities aged 15 and over in Canada were in poverty. That uses the Market Basket Measure (2023 base), the official poverty line, for all persons. The estimates cover the ten provinces and exclude the territories.

A provincial figure could come from a custom tabulation of the Canadian Income Survey, or from its public-use microdata. I haven't run either.

```json
{"values": [{"name": "Poverty rate, persons with disabilities aged 15+, Canada (MBM 2023 base) – national proxy, not Alberta", "value": 12.6, "unit": "%", "period": "2024"}], "sources": [{"publisher": "Statistics Canada", "id": "Table 11-10-0090-01, vector v1793292452"}], "not_published": true, "abstain": false, "abstain_reason": "Table 11-10-0090-01 has Canada-level data only; no Alberta estimate was found."}
```

Ontario's employment rate was higher than Quebec's in September 2026, but only by a small margin. These are seasonally adjusted rates for people aged 15 and over.

- **Ontario:** 60.1%
- **Quebec:** 59.9%

The gap is 0.2 percentage points. The standard error on each rate is about 0.3, so the difference is within sampling error and may not be statistically significant.

The unadjusted rates reverse the order. Quebec was 60.2% and Ontario 59.9%.

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 14-10-0287-01 (Labour Force Survey), released 2026-11-06. Ontario is vector v2063951 and Quebec is v2063762.

],

In August 2026, Canada's job vacancy rate was 2.8%, with 507,220 vacant positions. These are seasonally adjusted figures, and the rate was also 2.8% in July. The August data were released on 2026-10-29. The table didn't return quality flags for these values.

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 14-10-0432-01. The vacancies series is v1481212145 and the rate series is v1481212147.

```json
{"values":[{"name":"Job vacancy rate, Canada (seasonally adjusted)","value":2.8,"unit":"%","period":"2026-08"},{"name":"Job vacancies, Canada (seasonally adjusted)","value":507220,"unit":"positions","period":"2026-08"}],"sources":[{"publisher":"Statistics Canada","id":"14-10-0432-01; v1481212145; v1481212147"}],"not_published":false,"abstain":false,"abstain_reason":""}
```

**Prince Edward Island** had the highest 12-month CPI inflation in September 2026, at **5.7%**. The index was 177.6, up 5.65% from a year earlier. I computed this from the published index levels, so StatCan's own rounded figure may differ slightly.

Nova Scotia was a close second at 5.6% (index 178.1, up 5.63%). Canada overall was 3.1%.

This is all-items CPI, not seasonally adjusted. The territories aren't in the ranking because the table only publishes Whitehorse and Yellowknife, not territory-wide figures.

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 18-10-0004-01, all-items CPI. The PEI vector is v41691379, and the Nova Scotia vector is v41691513. The reference period is September 2026.

```json
{"values": [
{"name": "Highest 12-month CPI inflation among provinces: Prince Edward Island", "value": 5.65, "unit": "%", "period": "2026-09"},
{"name": "PEI all-items CPI index (2002=100)", "value": 177.6, "unit": "index", "period": "2026-09"},
{"name": "Nova Scotia 12-month CPI inflation (second highest)", "value": 5.63, "unit": "%", "period": "2026-09"},
{"name": "Canada 12-month CPI inflation", "value": 3.09, "unit": "%", "period": "2026-09"}
],
"sources": [{"publisher": "Statistics Canada", "id": "Table 18-10-0004-01, vector v41691379 (PEI)"}],
"not_published": false,
"abstain": false,
"abstain_reason": ""}
```

Canada's real GDP grew at an annualized rate of **3.3%** in Q2 2026. That is the seasonally adjusted, chained (2017) dollar figure as first published on 2026-08-28. The quarter-over-quarter change was 0.8%. Q1 2026 was revised to +0.1% (0.3% annualized).

The first-published figure may have been revised since. The Q3 2026 release is scheduled for November 30, and I didn't check for revisions to Q2.

Source: Statistics Canada, Daily release "Gross domestic product, income and expenditure, second quarter 2026", Table 3 (based on table 36-10-0104-01). I did not pull the vector ID.

```json
{"values":[{"name":"Real GDP growth, annualized quarter-to-quarter","value":3.3,"unit":"%","period":"Q2 2026"},{"name":"Real GDP growth, quarter-to-quarter","value":0.8,"unit":"%","period":"Q2 2026"},{"name":"Real GDP growth, annualized, Q1 2026 (revised)","value":0.3,"unit":"%","period":"Q1 2026"}],"sources":[{"publisher":"Statistics Canada","id":"36-10-0104-01"},{"publisher":"Statistics Canada","id":"The Daily dq260828a, Table 3"}],"not_published":false,"abstain":false,"abstain_reason":""}
```

The total value of building permits issued in Canada in August 2026 was **about $13.43 billion**. That is the seasonally adjusted figure in current dollars, which is the series Statistics Canada leads with. The value is $13,429,718 thousand.

- **Unadjusted:** the August value was about $13.00 billion ($12,997,151 thousand).
- **Revisions:** these figures come from the 12 November 2026 release, which covers September 2026 and revises earlier months. Statistics Canada may have revised August since it was first published.

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 34-10-0292-01, "Building permits, by type of structure and type of work". The seasonally adjusted series is vector v1675119645 and the unadjusted series is v1675115467. Both are for Canada, total residential and non-residential, all types of work.

```json
{"values": [{"name": "Total value of building permits, Canada, seasonally adjusted, current dollars", "value": 13429718, "unit": "thousand dollars (about $13.43 billion)", "period": "2026-08"}, {"name": "Total value of building permits, Canada, unadjusted, current dollars", "value": 12997151, "unit": "thousand dollars (about $13.00 billion)", "period": "2026-08"}], "sources": [{"publisher": "Statistics Canada", "id": "Table 34-10-0292-01, vector v1675119645 (SA), v1675115467 (unadjusted)"}], "not_published": false, "abstain": false, "abstain_reason": ""}
```

Canada had a merchandise trade surplus of **$4.95 billion** with the world in August 2026. This is the seasonally adjusted, balance-of-payments basis, which is the headline measure. The figure is in current dollars.

The value is the latest vintage, released 2026-11-04 alongside September data. September's surplus was $5.35 billion. July's was $0.91 billion. The August figure may differ from what was first published, because earlier months get revised.

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 12-10-0011-01, vector v87008984 (Trade Balance, all countries).

```json
{"values": [{"name": "Canada merchandise trade balance with all countries (BoP basis, seasonally adjusted)", "value": 4951.3, "unit": "millions of CAD", "period": "2026-08"}, {"name": "Trade balance, September 2026 (for context)", "value": 5350.1, "unit": "millions of CAD", "period": "2026-09"}, {"name": "Trade balance, July 2026 (for context)", "value": 905.3, "unit": "millions of CAD", "period": "2026-07"}], "sources": [{"publisher": "Statistics Canada", "id": "Table 12-10-0011-01, vector v87008984"}], "not_published": false, "abstain": false, "abstain_reason": ""}
```

Applying the September 2026 unemployment rate to the 2021 Census labour force gives about **1.26 million unemployed Canadians**.

- 2021 Census labour force (Canada, population 15 and over): 19,310,345 people.
- September 2026 unemployment rate (seasonally adjusted): 6.5%.
- Calculation: 19,310,345 × 0.065 ≈ 1,255,172.

This is only an approximation. It mixes the 2021 Census labour force with a 2026 rate, and the labour force has changed since 2021. The Labour Force Survey publishes its own unemployed count for September 2026, which is the better figure. I didn't retrieve it.

The latest rate is October 2026, at 6.7%. I used September because you asked for it.

The census count is randomly rounded. The arithmetic is mine, because the calculation tool only accepts series references, not raw numbers.

```json
{"values": [
{"name": "Labour force, Canada (2021 Census)", "value": 19310345, "unit": "persons", "period": "May 2021 (Census day)"},
{"name": "Unemployment rate, Canada, seasonally adjusted", "value": 6.5, "unit": "%", "period": "September 2026"},
{"name": "Implied unemployed (census labour force x Sept 2026 rate)", "value": 1255172, "unit": "persons", "period": "2021 Census labour force with September 2026 rate"}
],
"sources": [
{"publisher": "Statistics Canada", "id": "2021 Census Profile, characteristic 2224 'In the labour force', Canada (DGUID 2021A000011124)"},
{"publisher": "Statistics Canada", "id": "Table 14-10-0287-01, vector v2062815"}
],
"not_published": false,
"abstain": false,
"abstain_reason": ""}
```

Canada's CPI time base is **2002=100**. It replaced 1992=100 starting with the **May 2007 CPI**, which was released in June 2007. I'm answering from memory and didn't check this against a Statistics Canada source or table in this session. I also didn't check whether the base has changed since then. As far as I know, 2002=100 is still the base.
